standard.title: Designed products and environments
standard.description: explore how familiar products, services and environments are designed by people
standard.prior_knowledge: This is the first Design and Technologies descriptor in the curriculum. Students have no prior DT knowledge assumed. They bring general familiarity with everyday products and environments. They have not yet connected objects or places to the idea that people deliberately designed and made them for a purpose.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore how familiar products, services and environments are designed by people, identifying that design decisions are made for a purpose.

nodes.label: Recognising that products and environments are designed by people
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify familiar products and environments and recognise that they were designed and made by people
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two familiar products or environments (e.g. playground, packaging, school building) and state that people designed and made them
nodes.typical_width: Identify multiple familiar products, services and environments across home and school contexts; explain that each was designed by people; recognise that different things are designed for different reasons
wider: Identify how First Nations Australians have long designed and produced domestic items — for example exploring how the Lamalama Peoples weave bags using fibres from two different plants; discuss what the item was designed for and how the design choices reflect purpose
Explore how a local playground has shade structures designed to protect users and allow access for all — identify specific design decisions and explain why they were made

response_modes.reason: Students at Foundation may not distinguish between natural objects and designed objects, or may not yet connect a familiar thing (the school building, their lunch box) to the idea that a person made deliberate decisions about it. Accumulating examples across product, service and environment categories builds the category of 'designed by people' before purpose reasoning is introduced.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations domestic items direction is rich — it grounds the concept of design in purposeful, culturally situated production that predates industrial manufacturing, making the 'designed by people' idea concrete and broad.
success_criteria: Names at least two designed products or environments
States that people designed and made them — does not treat them as naturally occurring
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a populated category of 'designed by people', Node 2's purpose reasoning has no grounded examples to work with — students cannot explore why design decisions were made if they have not yet reliably identified that objects are designed at all.

nodes.label: Exploring design decisions and purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore how a product, service or environment is designed for a purpose — identifying at least one design decision and why it was made
nodes.minimum_width: For one familiar product or environment, identify one design decision and explain what purpose it serves
nodes.typical_width: Explore design decisions across multiple products, services and environments; explain how design decisions (materials, shape, features) serve the purpose; ask questions about why things were designed the way they were
wider: Ask questions about the design of products from the local store — why was particular packaging chosen? how do the text and images attract people's attention? connect design decisions to purpose
Explore how community gardens, public swimming pools and parks are designed to help people stay healthy — identify specific design decisions and the purposes they serve
Explore how an online or delivery service is designed to meet people's needs — describe how gift packages are sent between locations and how design decisions make this possible

response_modes.reason: Connecting a design decision to its purpose requires students to reason from feature to intent — 'the shade structure is there because...' rather than just noticing the shade structure exists. Scaffolding this with a question structure (what is it? who uses it? what does this part do? why?) builds the reasoning habit before the Y1-2 descriptor asks students to connect design to community need and sustainability.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one design decision in a product or environment
Connects that decision to a purpose — explains why it was designed that way
